records.table: The Kaku Highball begins with Kakubin, the square bottled Suntory blend of 1937 that marries Yamazaki and Hakushu malts with Chita grain. Squeeze lemon over heaped ice, add one part whisky to four of chilled soda, and it drinks light and dry: lemon, green apple and toasted nuts.
records.story: Yamazaki, which Shinjiro Torii (1879 to 1962) began building in 1923, sent out its first whisky, Shirofuda, in 1929. By Suntory's account Torii, whose Osaka business became Suntory, then set out as its first master blender to make a gentler blend that suited Japanese taste, and in 1937 it came out, sold simply as Suntory Whisky. The square bottle was shaped for easy storage and cut with an auspicious tortoiseshell pattern, an idea the house traces to a cut glass Satsuma kiriko perfume bottle; drinkers named it Kakubin, square bottle, and the nickname became the whisky's name. In the 1950s highballs filled the Torys whisky bars, and from 2008 a Suntory campaign for the Kakubin highball brought whisky back to tables across Japan. The drink is the Kaku Highball, Kaku-hai in Japan, named for the bottle, and Suntory's recipe keeps to one method: lemon first, heaped ice, cold soda poured slowly. The Japanese highball is learnt on Kakubin: a light, dry blend built to keep its shape under ice and soda.

records.table: Twenty-four facets are cut into the bottle of Hibiki Japanese Harmony, Suntory's blend with no age statement: Yamazaki and Hakushu malts married to Chita grain. Rose, lychee and honey open it, then candied orange and a hint of Mizunara oak; pour it neat or over a single large cube.
records.story: Hibiki came out in 1989 to mark the ninetieth year of the Osaka business that Shinjiro Torii (1879 to 1962) founded and that grew into Suntory. The name means resonance. The blend joined malts from Yamazaki and Hakushu with grain whisky from Chita, so that every part came from the house's own stills; Japanese firms rarely exchange whisky with one another, so a Suntory blender works from Suntory's own malts and grains. From 1989 the bottle was designed around the number twenty-four: its twenty-four facets stand, by Suntory's account, for the twenty-four seasons of the old Japanese calendar. For years the range was known by its age statements, the 17 and the 21. In 2015 Suntory added Japanese Harmony, a blend with no age statement drawing about ten malt and grain whiskies from five kinds of cask, Mizunara oak among them. In 2018 Suntory paused the 17, with too little seventeen-year-old whisky left in its warehouses. Japanese Harmony is the Hibiki a bar is likely to hold, and it shows how one house builds a whole from its own malts and grain.

records.story: Suntory's blends often take Yamazaki malt, the house's first, as their key part. Toki, whose name means time in Japanese, turned that order round. Suntory brought it out in the United States in August 2016, carrying no age statement and led by two whiskies: Hakushu malt aged in American white oak, from the forest distillery Suntory founded in 1973, and heavy-type grain whisky from Chita. Yamazaki malts from American white oak and Spanish oak casks play the supporting part, by Suntory's account, rounding the blend and lifting the sweetness of the grain. The house says the name speaks both of its whisky-making traditions and of the new approach to blending it took here. Toki was made to be poured many ways, neat, on the rocks and in cocktails, but above all long, and Suntory's own serve fills a tall glass to the brim with ice before the soda goes in. Keep Toki on the rail for highballs: green, light and clean, it is also a plain introduction to how a Japanese blender balances malt against grain.

records.story: Nikka began on Hokkaido in 1934, when Masataka Taketsuru (1894 to 1979), who had learnt whisky making in Scotland, founded Dai Nippon Kaju at Yoichi; the name Nikka is drawn from it, and apple juice was its trade while its first spirit matured in cask. Its malt came from Yoichi's coal-fired stills and, from 1969, from Miyagikyo near Sendai, where Nikka's Coffey stills came to make its grain whisky. From the Barrel came out in 1985, after the founder's death, when, by the brand's account, Nikka's blenders set out to catch the whisky as it comes from the cask. More than a hundred malt and grain whiskies are blended, returned to cask to marry for some months, and bottled at 51.4 per cent with little water added. The squat square bottle, designed in 1985 as a small block of whisky, has barely changed since. By Nikka's own history it was sold at first only in Hokkaido and Aomori, and across Japan from 1988. Under the makers' association standard set in 2021, Nikka states that this blend does not meet every criterion of Japanese whisky, and says so on its own pages. A blend can be dense and strong, and this one proves it: a lot of whisky in a small bottle.

records.story: The bottle carries the name of Masataka Taketsuru (1894 to 1979), from a sake-brewing family in Takehara, who learnt whisky making in Scotland and in 1934 founded at Yoichi, on Hokkaido, the company that became Nikka. Yoichi's coal-fired stills gave a heavy, smoky malt; Miyagikyo, near Sendai, followed in 1969 and gave a softer, fruitier one, so that the house held two malts of different character to blend. Taketsuru Pure Malt brings that pairing together under his name. Nikka uses pure malt only for whiskies blended from its own malts, what Scotland calls a blended malt: no grain whisky goes in. The Taketsuru Pure Malt name reached the shelf in 2000, and Pure Malts of seventeen, twenty-one and twenty-five years followed. In 2020 Nikka withdrew those three and kept the no-age-statement Pure Malt at 43 per cent, in a renewed blend. Coal-fired Yoichi brings weight and peat, steam-heated Miyagikyo fruit and softness, and sherry casks from both stand among the key malts. Two distilleries of one house, married without grain: that is the other kind of blend, and the lesson of this bottle.
